messages.content: Write an internal post about making security everyone's responsibility at a software company. Around 250 words.

output:
**Security isn't the security team's job**

There are four of us on the security team. There are roughly 180 people shipping code. Do the math on that ratio and you'll see why the review-queue model was never going to hold — last quarter we sat on 61 pull requests for an average of nine days each, and two of the incidents we had came from code that had passed our review anyway.

So we're changing how this works.

Starting next sprint, security review moves to the team that owns the service. You know your data flows; we don't, not really. What we'll do instead is give you the tooling and the answers: threat-model templates that take twenty minutes, a Slack channel where someone from the team responds inside an hour, and office hours on Tuesdays for the gnarly stuff.

Three things we're asking for. Model the threat before you design, not after. Treat a dependency bump like a code change, because it is one. And when you find something ugly in your own service, file it — nobody gets blamed for reporting. We mean that; if it turns out we don't mean it, tell my manager.

The parts that stay with us: incident response, pen tests, the auth libraries, and anything touching customer payment data. Escalate those, don't handle them.

This will be worse before it's better. You'll file findings that turn out to be nothing, and we'll write guidance that turns out to be wrong. Fine. Nine-day review queues are worse.

Questions to #security-eng.
